label: thm:negative
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:negative}
There exists an integer $N_0$ such that, for every integer $N\ge N_0$,
the polynomial $F_N$ in \eqref{eq:FN} is nonnegative but is not a finite
sum of squares of real homogeneous quadratic polynomials.
An explicit sufficient value of $N_0$ is given in
\Cref{prop:explicit-threshold}.
head: environment

label: lem:frame
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Complete characterization of wedge Gram representations

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $F=\sum_jq_j^2$. Evaluating at $y=0$ shows that every
$q_j(x,0)$ vanishes identically, and evaluating at $x=0$ gives the
analogous conclusion. Thus $q_j=x^\top A_jy$ for a real matrix $A_j$.
The identity $q_j(x,x)=0$ implies $A_j+A_j^\top=0$, whence
$q_j=\sum_{a<b}(A_j)_{ab}z_{ab}$. The coefficient vectors of the
$q_j$ give a positive semidefinite Gram matrix. 
To determine the relation space, group products of wedges by their
multisets of labels. Monomials belonging to different multisets cannot
cancel. For a multiset with a repeated label, there is at most one
nonzero wedge product up to sign, and that product is not the zero
polynomial. For four distinct labels, the three possible products are
$z_{ab}z_{cd}$, $z_{ac}z_{bd}$ and $z_{ad}z_{bc}$. Any two are linearly
independent, as is seen by comparing their coefficients, whereas their
alternating combination in \eqref{eq:plucker} vanishes. Their relation
space is therefore exactly one-dimensional. This proves the asserted
description of the correction space. 
Any representing Gram matrix differs from $G$ by an element of this
space. Conversely, a positive semidefinite representative factors as
$R^\top R$, and the rows of $Rz$ provide the required quadratic factors.
This proves \eqref{eq:frame}.
head: environment

label: lem:corner
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:corner}
Let $X$ and $Y$ be corner-supported Toeplitz matrices of size $N$ and
depth $m$, with $N\ge 2m$, and let $\mathcal F_m$ be the restricted
B\"ottcher--Wenzel form defined in \eqref{eq:Bm-definition}.  Let
$
 z=(z_{ab})_{a<b},
 z_{ab}:=x_a y_b-x_b y_a,
$
be the full wedge vector defined in \eqref{wedge coordinate}, and let
\begin{equation}
\label{restricted wedge coordinate}
 z_r:=(z_{ab})_{
 a,b\in\Lambda_{N,m},\,a<b}
 \in\mathbb{R}^{\binom{2m}{2}}
\end{equation}
be its restriction to the retained labels.
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If
$
        F_N=z^\top Gz
$
is any Gram representation in the full wedge coordinates, then
\[
        \mathcal F_m=z_r^\top G_rz_r,
\]
where $G_r$ is the principal submatrix of $G$ indexed by the retained
wedge coordinates.

\item
After identifying the retained labels by their side and depth
$p=0,\ldots,m-1$, the polynomial $\mathcal F_m$ depends only on $m$ and
is independent of $N$.

\item
If $\mathcal F_m$ is not SoS, then $F_N$ is not SoS for every
$N\ge2m$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Properties of the corner-supported Toeplitz BW form

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first statement, setting $x_a=y_a=0$ for $a\notin\Lambda_{N,m}$ annihilates every wedge containing a non-retained label. Hence $z^\top Gz$ restricts directly to $z_r^\top G_rz_r$.

For the second statement, let $U_a$ be the shift matrix $(U_a)_{ij}=\mathbf{1}_{i-j=a}$, $0\le i,j<N$. Distinct shifts are Frobenius orthogonal and $\|U_a\|_F^2=N-|a|$. The weighted Lagrange identity \cite[Lemma~10]{laszlo2012} and bilinearity of the commutator give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:literal-gram}
 F_N=
 2\sum_{a<b}(N-|a|)(N-|b|)z_{ab}^2
 -
 \Bigl\|\sum_{a<b}z_{ab}[U_a,U_b]\Bigr\|_F^2.
\end{equation}
For a retained label, $N-|\pm(N-1-a)|=a+1$. Shifts on the same side commute, while for $C_{ab}:=[U_{-(N-1-a)},U_{N-1-b}]$ one has, for $N\ge2m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutator-overlap}
 \langle C_{ab},C_{cd}\rangle_F
 =
 2\mathbf{1}_{a-b=c-d}\min(a+1,b+1,c+1,d+1).
\end{equation}
Thus every coefficient of the restricted quartic depends only on the depths $a,b,c,d$, and hence only on $m$.

Finally, linear restriction preserves sums of squares. Therefore an SoS representation of $F_N$ would restrict to an SoS representation of $\mathcal F_m$, proving the last statement by contraposition.

label: lem:corner-gram
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:corner-gram}
Let $\mathcal{F}_m$ be a corner-supported Toeplitz B\"ottcher--Wenzel form
generated by two Toeplitz matrices $X,Y$ of size $N$ and corner depth
$m$, where $N\ge2m$.  
Collect the coordinates into
$z_r=(u^\top,v^\top,w^\top)^\top$, using lexicographic
order within each depth-indexed group.
                                                                                                                                                                                      
Then $\mathcal{F}_m$ admits the following block Gram representation:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:baseline-gram}
 \mathcal F_m=z_r^\top G_mz_r,\qquad
 G_m=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 D&K&0\\
 K&D&0\\
 0&0&B
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Here $D,K\in\mathbb S^{\binom m2}$ are symmetric positive definite,
and $B\in\mathbb S^{m^2}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite.
{                                 The blocks $D,K,B$ depend only on the corner depth $m$ and are independent of the matrix size $N$.}
head: environment
name: Gram representation of the corner-supported Toeplitz BW form

label: eq:exchange
title: Proof
body_md:
We rearrange the restricted expression \eqref{eq:literal-gram} using
the Pl\"ucker relations, as in the Gram construction of
\cite[Sections~2 and~5]{laszlo2012}.  The raw Gram couples mixed wedges
with equal differences $a-b=c-d$.  For $a<c$ and $b<d$ satisfying this
equality, the corresponding term is
$-4\min(a+1,b+1)w_{ab}w_{cd}$.  With the orientation above, the Pl\"ucker
identity becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exchange}
 u_{ac}v_{bd}+w_{ab}w_{cd}-w_{ad}w_{cb}=0,
\end{equation}
so that the mixed product is replaced by
$-u_{ac}v_{bd}+w_{ad}w_{cb}$.  Summing the resulting contributions gives
\eqref{eq:baselines}. 
Specifically, $D,K\in\mathbb S^{\binom m2}$,
$B\in\mathbb S^{m^2}$, and
$G_m\in\mathbb S^{m(2m-1)}$ where $
\mathbb S 
$
denotes the space of real symmetric matrices and the specific entries are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:baselines}
\begin{aligned}
 (D)_{ab,cd}
 &=2(a+1)(b+1)\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd}, \quad
 (K)_{ab,cd}
  =2\mathbf{1}_{b-a=d-c}\min(a+1,c+1),\\
 (B)_{ab,cd}
 &=2(a+1)(b+1)\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd}
 -2\mathbf{1}_{a+b=c+d}\min(a+1,b+1,c+1,d+1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $D,K$, the index pairs satisfy $0\le a<b<m$ and
$0\le c<d<m$; for $B$, all four indices range independently over
$\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$.  

Finally, $D\succ0$ follows immediately from its
strictly positive diagonal entries.
For $K$, its nonzero entries satisfy $b-a=d-c$.
For each fixed difference, the corresponding block
has entries $2\min(a+1,c+1)$. Since
\[
\min(a+1,c+1)
=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(a,c)}1,
\]
this block is the Gram matrix of linearly independent
cumulative-sum vectors, and hence is positive definite.
Thus $K\succ0$.
For $B$, its nonzero off-diagonal entries satisfy
$a+b=c+d$. Consider a complete block with
$a+b<m$, and fix a row indexed by $(a,b)$.
Its row sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(a+1)(b+1)
-2\sum_{j=0}^{a+b}
\min(a+1,b+1,j+1,a+b-j+1)
=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, the sum equals $(a+1)(b+1)$.
Since all off-diagonal entries are nonpositive,
each complete block is a positive semidefinite
weighted graph Laplacian.
The remaining truncated blocks are principal
submatrices of the corresponding complete blocks
and are therefore also positive semidefinite.
Consequently, $B\succeq0$.
head: environment

label: rem:baseline-positivity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:baseline-positivity}
An important feature and advantage of the Gram representation
\eqref{eq:baseline-gram} is that independently of whether $\mathcal{F}_m$
is SoS, we always have
$$
D,K\succ0 \qquad B\succeq0
$$ hold for every corner
depth $m\ge2${                                 .}
In other words, the positive definiteness of $D$ and $K$
does not guarantee that the full Gram matrix
$G_m$ is positive semidefinite, since $D-K$
need not be positive semidefinite.
head: environment
name: Positivity of the baseline blocks

label: lem:normal-form
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normal-form}
Let $\mathcal{F}_m$ be a corner-supported Toeplitz B\"ottcher--Wenzel form
generated by two Toeplitz matrices $X,Y$ of size $N$ and corner depth
$m$, where $N\ge2m$.  Then the following statements hold.
\begin{itemize}

\item The Gram representation of $\mathcal{F}_m$ is not unique.  If $\mathcal{F}_m$
admits a positive semidefinite Gram representation, then it admits a
symmetry-reduced representative of the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-gram-1}
 Q_{\rm av}=G_m+
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \mathcal E_0&\mathcal E_1&0\\
 \mathcal E_1&\mathcal E_0&0\\
 0&0&\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1
 \end{pmatrix}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 D+\mathcal E_0&K+\mathcal E_1&0\\
 K+\mathcal E_1&D+\mathcal E_0&0\\
 0&0&B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1
 \end{pmatrix}\succeq0,
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal E_0,\mathcal E_1\in\mathbb S^{\binom m2}$,
$\mathcal E_0$ is a same-side Pl\"ucker correction acting within each
pure wedge family (equivalently, a pure four-form),
$\mathcal E_1$ is a real symmetric matrix coupling the two pure wedge
families, and $\mathcal{R}$ is the realignment map induced by the corresponding
index re-pairing.\footnote{The full correction matrix is an element
$\mathcal E$ of the space characterized in Lemma~\ref{lem:frame};
$\mathcal E_0$ and $\mathcal E_1$ are the components remaining after
the symmetry reduction. The realignment operator
$
\mathcal{R}:\mathbb S^{\binom m2}\to\mathbb S^{m^2}
$
is a linear map that re-pairs the four indices of a pure-wedge Gram block into the corresponding mixed-wedge indices.  In particular, it maps a correction on the pure wedge space to the induced correction on the mixed wedge space. The induced mixed correction
$\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1$ belongs to $\mathbb S^{m^2}$.  See
Appendix \ref{app:normal-form-proof} for the detailed construction.}

\item Under the orthogonal change of coordinates
$(u,v,w)\mapsto((u+v)/\sqrt2,(u-v)/\sqrt2,w)$, the Gram representation
in \eqref{eq:general-gram-1} becomes block diagonal:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-gram-2}
 \widehat Q_{\rm av}
 :=U^\top Q_{\rm av}U
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 P_+&0&0\\
 0&P_-&0\\
 0&0&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \tag{Block-diag Gram}
\end{equation}
where $U$ is the orthogonal matrix representing the change of coordinates 
                     
    
     
                  
                                          
                                           
              
                 
                     
    
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sectors}
 P_\pm=D+\mathcal E_0\pm K\pm\mathcal E_1
 \in\mathbb S^{\binom m2},
 \qquad
 M=B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1\in\mathbb S^{m^2}.
\end{equation}

\item The corner-supported form satisfies
\[
 \mathcal{F}_m\text{ is SoS}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{there exist }\mathcal E_0,\mathcal E_1
 \text{ such that }Q_{\rm av}\succeq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P_+\succeq0,\quad P_-\succeq0,\quad M\succeq0.
\]
\end{itemize}

label: lem:finite-test
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Finite Gram test

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathcal F_m$ is SoS, Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-form} gives a normal-form
Gram representation with $\widehat Q_{\rm av}\succeq0$.  Hence, for every
$\hat y\in\mathbb{C}^s$,
\[
 \hat y^*\mathcal G_m\hat y
 =\hat y^*V^*\widehat Q_{\rm av}V\hat y
 =(V\hat y)^*\widehat Q_{\rm av}(V\hat y)\ge0.
\]
Thus $\mathcal G_m\succeq0$, and the last assertion follows by taking
$\hat y=c$.
head: environment

label: rem:complex-test
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:complex-test}
The original SoS problem and all Gram representations above remain over
the real numbers.  Complex numbers are introduced only in the test
points used below, and do not change the underlying real SoS problem.

Indeed, let $Q$ be a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix.  For
any complex vector $z=\hat u+i\hat v$, with
$\hat u,\hat v$ real, we have
\[
 z^*Qz
 =
 (\hat u^\top-i\hat v^\top)Q(\hat u+i\hat v)
 =
 \hat u^\top Q\hat u+\hat v^\top Q\hat v\ge0,
\]
where the cross terms cancel because $Q$ is symmetric.  Thus a real
positive semidefinite Gram matrix remains positive semidefinite when
tested against complex vectors.

We may therefore choose several complex test points and arrange their
corresponding feature vectors as the columns of a complex test matrix
$\mathcal V$.  The resulting matrix
$
\mathcal V^*Q\mathcal V
$
must still be positive semidefinite whenever $Q\succeq0$.  Allowing
complex test points gives us a larger and more flexible space of test
directions, without enlarging the class of admissible Gram
representations. 
In the construction in \Cref{sec choose direction}, we  will choose complex points that approach
$(i,-i)$ along prescribed directions as $m$ increases.  The associated
test matrix develops a strictly negative limiting direction $c$.  Since any
real SoS Gram representation would remain positive semidefinite under
the same complex test, this eventually yields the contradiction used to
prove that the corner-supported form is not SoS.
head: environment
name: Complex test points

label: lem:finite-decomposition
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Finite Gram decomposition

title: Proof
body_md:
From the block diagonal form of $\widehat Q_{\rm av}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal G_m
=
\left(
\begin{array}{ccc}
V_1^*/\sqrt2&
V_1^*/\sqrt2&
V_3^*
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{ccc}
P_+&0&0\\
0&P_-&0\\
0&0&M
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
V_1/\sqrt2\\
V_1/\sqrt2\\
V_3
\end{array}
\right)=
V_1^*\frac{P_++P_-}{2}V_1
+
V_3^*MV_3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using \eqref{eq:sectors},
$
(P_++P_-)/2=D+\mathcal E_0
$
and
$
M=B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1.
$
Moreover,
$
P_-=D-K+\mathcal E_0-\mathcal E_1
$
 and the pure four-form $\mathcal E_0$ is alternating\footnote{At the level of four-slot generating expressions, realignment exchanges the middle two arguments of the totally alternating form, and hence changes its sign. This does not identify the pure- and mixed-space matrices, which have different sizes; the identity used below holds for the matched feature evaluations.}.
At the level of the corresponding finite evaluations,
this gives
$
V_1^*\mathcal E_0V_1=-V_3^*(\mathcal{R} \mathcal E_0)V_3.
$
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal G_m
&=
V_1^*DV_1
+
V_3^*BV_3
-
V_3^*\mathcal{R}(\mathcal E_0-\mathcal E_1)V_3\\
&=
V_1^*DV_1
+
V_3^*
\bigl(B+\mathcal{R}(D-K)\bigr)V_3
-
V_3^*(\mathcal{R} P_-)V_3,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:finite-decomposition}.
head: environment

label: lem:negative-limit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:negative-limit}
Let $\mathbf L_m$ be defined as in
\Cref{lem:finite-decomposition}. Fix the test points in
\eqref{eq:test-nodes}. Then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}

\item As $m\to\infty$,
$
\mathsf x_\ell^{(m)}\to(i,-i)
$
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L-limit}
        \frac{1}{m^2}\mathbf L_m\longrightarrow\mathbf L_\star,
\end{equation}
where
$
\mathbf L_\star\in\mathbb S^s
$
is a fixed real symmetric $s\times s$ matrix, independent of $m$.

\item There exist a constant $\gamma>0$ and an integer $m_0>0$
such that
$
        \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)<-\gamma<0.
$
Let $c_\star\in\mathbb{R}^s$ be a corresponding real unit eigenvector.
Since $\mathbf L_\star$ is independent of $m$, the same
$c_\star$ is used for every $m\ge m_0$.

\item There exists an integer $m_1\ge m_0$ such that, for every
$m\ge m_1$, defining
$
\widetilde c_m:=c_\star/m,
$
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L-negative-limit}
 \widetilde c_m^*\mathbf L_m\widetilde c_m
 < -\frac{\gamma}{2}<0.
\end{equation}

\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Negative limit of the Gram-invariant part

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the three statements in order. 
For the first statement, the entries of $\mathbf L_m$ are explicit finite
sums determined by $D,K,B$ and the points $\mathsf x_\ell^{(m)}$. Since
$
\mathsf x_\ell^{(m)}\to(i,-i)
$
at rate $m^{-1/2}$, the corresponding expressions have a leading term
of order $m^2$; see \Cref{B:lem:scaled-limit}. For $1\le\ell,h\le s$, define
\[
 A_{\ell h}:=
 |a_\ell+\overline{a_h}|^2,
 \qquad
 C_{\ell h}:=
 4\,\Re(a_\ell)\Re(a_h).
\]
Expanding the leading term gives
\[
 \frac{1}{m^2}(\mathbf L_m)_{\ell h}
 \longrightarrow
 2\left(
 \frac{2}{A_{\ell h}^2}
 +\frac{1}{C_{\ell h}^2}
 -\frac{1}{A_{\ell h}C_{\ell h}}
 \right)
 =:(\mathbf L_\star)_{\ell h}.
\]
Thus
$
 \mathbf L_\star:=
 \left[
 2\left(
 \frac{2}{A_{\ell h}^2}
 +\frac{1}{C_{\ell h}^2}
 -\frac{1}{A_{\ell h}C_{\ell h}}
 \right)
 \right]_{\ell,h=1}^s
 \in\mathbb S^s
$
is a fixed real symmetric $s\times s$ matrix, independent of $m$.
Since $s$ is fixed, entrywise convergence implies convergence in
any matrix norm, proving
$
        \frac{1}{m^2}\mathbf L_m\longrightarrow\mathbf L_\star.
$

\noindent

\noindent
\textbf{For the second statement}, the fixed two-family choice of
test points determines $\mathbf L_\star$ completely.
At $s=1024$, a direct floating-point diagonalization gives
$
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)\approx-1.18428\times10^{-2}.
$
To establish strict negativity rigorously independently of floating-point
accuracy, \Cref{B:lem:witness} provides an explicit
rational certificate proving
$
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)<-\gamma<0.
$
Let $c_\star\in\mathbb{R}^s$ be a corresponding real unit eigenvector:
\[
 \mathbf L_\star c_\star
 =\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)c_\star,
 \qquad c_\star^*c_\star=1.
\]
The matrix $\mathbf L_\star$, the constant $\gamma$, and the vector
$c_\star$ are fixed and independent of $m$. Choose $m_0$
sufficiently large that the asymptotic estimates below are valid,
and define
$
\widetilde c_m:=c_\star/m
$
for every $m\ge m_0$.

\noindent
\textbf{For the third statement,}
\[
 \widetilde c_m^*\mathbf L_m\widetilde c_m
 =
 c_\star^*
 \left(\frac{\mathbf L_m}{m^2}\right)c_\star
 \longrightarrow
 c_\star^*\mathbf L_\star c_\star
 =
 \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)
 <-\gamma.
\]
Therefore there exists an integer $m_1\ge m_0$ such that, for every
$m\ge m_1$,
$
 \widetilde c_m^*\mathbf L_m\widetilde c_m
 < -\frac{\gamma}{2}<0.
$
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: prop:R-vanishes
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Uniform vanishing of the Gram-dependent part

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the result in four steps. The uniform
tail estimates are established in \Cref{C:lem:conjugate},
while the analytic continuation is proved in
\Cref{C:lem:continuation}.

\paragraph{Step 1. Decomposition of the realigned Gram block.}
As defined in \eqref{eq:sectors},
$
P_-=D-K+\mathcal E_0-\mathcal E_1,
\quad
M=B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1,
$
and therefore
$
  \mathcal{R} P_-
 = \mathcal{R}(D-K)+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_0-(M-B).
$
For the test points
$\mathsf x_\ell=(\xi_\ell,\eta_\ell)\in\mathbb{C}^2$,
$1\le\ell\le s$, recall that
$\eta_\ell=\bar\xi_\ell$.
By the realignment identity, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RM-pure-evaluation}
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf R_m)_{\ell h}
&=[V_3^*(\mathcal{R} P_-)V_3]_{\ell h}  =f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)^*
P_-f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)
\\ &=
\underbrace{
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)^*(D-K)
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)
}_{:=\mathcal I_1}+
\underbrace{
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)^*\mathcal E_0
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)
}_{:=\mathcal I_2} -
\underbrace{
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)^*
\mathcal E_1
f(\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)
}_{:=\mathcal I_3}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here, $V_3$ is given in \eqref{eq:matched-features} and
$
f(\xi,\eta)
=
(\xi^a\eta^b-\xi^b\eta^a)_{0\le a<b<m}
$
is the pure-wedge feature vector. $(\mathbf R_m)_{\ell h}$ denotes the
$(\ell,h)$ entry of $\mathbf R_m$.
The three terms will be estimated using the
repeated/conjugate evaluations in Steps 2--3,
followed by analytic continuation in Step 4.
The first term $\mathcal I_1$ is determined by the fixed
matrices $D,K$; it is Gram invariant and is fixed
for every given polynomial. The second is a pure
four-form correction, while the third is the
pure cross-family correction, whose realignment
is constrained by $M\succeq0$.

\paragraph{Step 2. $\mathcal I_3$ has only
high-total-degree terms under repeated evaluation.}

We first claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:grouped-low-vanishing}
\sum_{\substack{a+b=\iota\\c+d=\kappa}}
(M-B)_{ab,cd}=0
\quad\text{whenever }\iota<m\text{ or }\kappa<m.
\end{equation}
Here $\iota,\kappa$ denote the total degrees of the
row and column indices, respectively, with
$0\le\iota,\kappa\le2m-2$.
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:high-order-I3}
\begin{aligned}
 v_3(t,t)^*(M-B)v_3(z,z) =
\sum_{a,b,c,d}
\bar t^{\,a+b}(M-B)_{ab,cd}z^{c+d} =
\sum_{\iota,\kappa\ge m}
\left(
\sum_{\substack{a+b=\iota\\c+d=\kappa}}
(M-B)_{ab,cd}
\right)
\bar t^{\,\iota}z^\kappa.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This expression only contains high-total-degree terms.
Intuitively, for the $m=2$ example in
\Cref{ex:normal-form-m2}, we have
\[
B=
\left(
\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
\color{teal}{0}&0&0&0\\ \hline
0&\color{teal}{2}&\color{teal}{-2}&0\\
0&\color{teal}{-2}&\color{teal}{2}&0\\ \hline
0&0&0&4
\end{array}
\right),
\qquad
M(\theta)=
\left(
\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
\color{orange}{0}&0&0&\color{orange}{\theta}\\ \hline
0&\color{orange}{2}&\color{orange}{-2-\theta}&0\\
0&\color{orange}{-2-\theta}&2&0\\ \hline
\color{orange}{\theta}&0&0&4
\end{array}
\right).
\]
The partitions correspond to the total degrees
$0,1,1,2$ of the mixed coordinates\footnote{
For $B$, the degree-$(0,0)$ block is zero,
and the complete degree-$(1,1)$ block
has total sum
$
2+(-2)+(-2)+2=0.
$
For $M(\theta)$, the corresponding low-degree
grouped coefficients include
the $(0,2)$-, $(1,1)$-, and $(2,0)$-blocks,
$
[\theta, 2+(-2-\theta)+(-2-\theta)+2, \theta]
$
respectively.
If $M(\theta)\succeq0$,
its zero $(00,00)$ diagonal entry forces
$M_{00,11}=\theta=0$.}.
Thus all low-total-degree grouped coefficients
vanish for $B$ and a feasible $M(\theta)$.

To prove the claim, recall from
\Cref{lem:corner-gram} that $B\succeq0$.
Its entries vanish between different total degrees,
and each complete total-degree block has zero
row sums. Hence
$
\sum_{\substack{a+b=\iota\\c+d=\kappa}}
B_{ab,cd}=0
\quad\text{if }\iota<m\text{ or }\kappa<m.
$
Now suppose that $M\succeq0$. Under the
repeated-node substitution,
$
v_3(t,t)=(t^{a+b})_{0\le a,b<m},
$
all pure wedges vanish. Since
$M=B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1$ represents the same
restricted polynomial on this substitution,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:repeated-mixed-identity}
v_3(t,t)^\top Mv_3(t,t)
=
v_3(t,t)^\top Bv_3(t,t).
\end{equation}
By the complete-block structure of $B$, the
right-hand side has no terms of degree below $2m$. Using the assumption that $\mathcal{F}_m$ is SoS\footnote{{                                 See \Cref{rem:sos-assumption} for details.}} and $M \succeq 0$ by \Cref{lem:normal-form}, we factor $M=T_M^\top T_M$. Since
$
v_3(t,t)^\top Mv_3(t,t)
=
\|T_Mv_3(t,t)\|^2,
$
every component of the polynomial vector
$T_Mv_3(t,t)$
must have vanishing coefficients of degree less
than $m$. Otherwise, choosing the smallest
degree $\iota_0<m$ with a nonzero coefficient
would produce a strictly positive coefficient
of $t^{2\iota_0}$ in the sum of squares,
contradicting \eqref{eq:repeated-mixed-identity}.
Consequently, the two-variable evaluation
$
v_3(t,t)^*Mv_3(z,z)
=
(T_Mv_3(t,t))^*(T_Mv_3(z,z))
$
contains only powers $\bar t^{\,\iota}z^\kappa$
with $\iota,\kappa\ge m$. The same property
holds for $B$, proving
\eqref{eq:grouped-low-vanishing}.
By direct multiplication, this also establishes
\eqref{eq:high-order-I3}.


\paragraph{Step 3. On the conjugate slice:
$\mathcal I_1=O(m)$ and $\mathcal I_2=0$.}

We now consider the pure-wedge feature vector
$
f(\xi,\bar\xi)
=
(\xi^a\bar\xi^b-\xi^b\bar\xi^a)_{0\le a<b<m}.
$
At the conjugate points $(\xi,\bar\xi)$,
the pure four-form correction vanishes under
the corresponding quadratic evaluation:
\[
\mathcal I_2 =
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*\mathcal E_0
f(\xi,\bar\xi)=0.
\]
The first term $\mathcal I_1=O(m)$ since it is
explicit with $D,K$ defined in \eqref{eq:baselines}
and sample points defined in \eqref{eq:test-nodes}; see \Cref{C:lem:conjugate}.
More precisely, writing sample points
$\xi=\sqrt{\rho}\,e^{i\vartheta}$ where $\rho=e^{-2\alpha/\sqrt m}$ and
$\vartheta=\pi/2-\beta/\sqrt m$, then as $m \rightarrow \infty$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal I_1
=
\frac{8\rho\sin^2\vartheta}
{(1-\rho)^2
\bigl((1-\rho)^2+4\rho\sin^2\vartheta\bigr)^2}
+o(m)\sim
\frac{8}{(4\alpha^2/m)\cdot16}
= \frac{m}{8\alpha^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here the rational expression is obtained from the
infinite-depth generating series, while the
finite-depth truncation error is exponentially small.
 

With
$\alpha,\beta$ in fixed real compact intervals
and $\alpha>0$, the finite-depth tail is
exponentially small. Hence
$
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*(D-K)f(\xi,\bar\xi)=O(m).
$
Recall that
$P_-=D-K+\mathcal E_0-\mathcal E_1$ and by \eqref{eq:RM-pure-evaluation},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pminus-repeated-identity}
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf R_m)_{\ell \ell} =
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*P_-f(\xi,\bar\xi)
=
\underbrace{
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*(D-K)f(\xi,\bar\xi)
}_{O(m)} +
\underbrace{
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*\mathcal E_0
f(\xi,\bar\xi)
}_{=0} +
\underbrace{
v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)^*(M-B)
v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)
}_{\text{high-total-degree tail}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here $\xi=\xi_\ell$ and
$\bar\xi=\eta_\ell$ for the diagonal entry.
The last equality uses the realignment identity
to rewrite the contribution of $-\mathcal E_1$. 
The third term in
\eqref{eq:Pminus-repeated-identity} contains only
high-total-degree contributions.
Positivity of $M$ and the fixed diagonal of $B$
give uniform bounds on the entries of $M-B$,
independent of the Gram corrections.
Consequently, for the prescribed scaled
conjugate nodes, the high-total-degree
tail is $o(m)$, uniformly over all feasible Gram
representations, by \Cref{C:lem:conjugate}. Combining the three terms gives
$
f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*P_-f(\xi,\bar\xi)=O(m).
$


\paragraph{Step 4. Analytic continuation to the realigned
test points.}

The $O(m)$ estimate in Step 3 applies only to
conjugate pairs $(\xi,\bar\xi)$. However, the
entries of $\mathbf R_m$ involve the generally
nonconjugate pairs $(\xi_\ell,\overline{\xi_h})$
when $\ell\ne h$.
To extend the estimate, using the SoS assumption and $P_- \succeq0$
by \Cref{lem:normal-form}, factor
$P_-=\Gamma^\top\Gamma$ and define
\[
h_m(\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac1m\Gamma f\left(
ie^{-(\alpha+i\beta)/\sqrt m},
-ie^{-(\alpha-i\beta)/\sqrt m}
\right).
\]
For real $\alpha,\beta$, Step 3 gives
$\|h_m(\alpha,\beta)\|^2=O(m^{-1})$,
while the general PSD bound gives
$\|h_m\|^2=O(1)$ on fixed complex rectangles.
Since $h_m$ is holomorphic in both variables,
the two-constant principle, applied successively
in $\alpha$ and $\beta$, propagates the vanishing
bound to the required complex region; see
\Cref{C:lem:continuation}.
Indeed, 
$
(\mathbf R_m)_{\ell h}
=
\|\Gamma f(\xi_\ell,\overline{\xi_h})\|^2.
$
These pairs correspond to the complex parameters
\[
\alpha_{\ell h}
=\frac{a_\ell+\overline{a_h}}2,
\qquad
\beta_{\ell h}
=\frac{a_\ell-\overline{a_h}}{2i},
\]
which by construction in \eqref{eq:test-nodes} {                                 satisfy}
\[
1\le\Re\alpha_{\ell h}\le2,\quad
|\Im\alpha_{\ell h}|\le256,\quad
|\Re\beta_{\ell h}|\le256,\quad
|\Im\beta_{\ell h}|\le\tfrac12.
\]
{                                 Thus all the test pairs lie in the continuation region, and
$m^{-2}\max_{\ell,h}|(\mathbf R_m)_{\ell h}|$ tends to zero uniformly over all feasible normal-form Gram representations.
Taking a nonnegative bound $\varepsilon_m\to0$ for these quantities gives \eqref{eq:R-uniform-limit}.}

label: rem:sos-assumption
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sos-assumption}
In the proof of \Cref{prop:R-vanishes}, assuming that
$\mathcal{F}_m$ is SoS allows us to conclude that $M, P_{\pm}\succeq0$
by \Cref{lem:normal-form}. Note that the positive
definiteness of $D,K$ and the positive semidefiniteness
of $B$ do not rely on this assumption, as these
properties hold for every corner depth $m\ge2$
by \Cref{lem:corner-gram}.
head: environment
name: Role of the SoS assumption

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$
M_0:=\max\{m_1,m_2\}
$
and suppose, for contradiction, that $\mathcal F_m$ is SoS for some
$m\ge M_0$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-test}, the corresponding finite
Gram test satisfies
$
\mathcal G_m\succeq0,
$
and therefore
$
        \widetilde c_m^*\mathcal G_m\widetilde c_m\ge0.
$
On the other hand, \Cref{lem:finite-decomposition,lem:negative-limit} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde c_m^*\mathcal G_m\widetilde c_m
&\le
\widetilde c_m^*\mathbf L_m\widetilde c_m
+
\left|
\widetilde c_m^*\mathbf R_m\widetilde c_m
\right| <
-\frac{\gamma}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{4}
=
-\frac{\gamma}{4}<0,
\end{aligned}
\]
contradicting $\mathcal G_m\succeq0$. Therefore $\mathcal F_m$ is not SoS for every sufficiently large corner
depth $m$.  In particular, choose any integer $m_\star\ge M_0$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:corner}, $\mathcal F_{m_\star}$ is a restriction of
$F_N$ for every $N\ge2m_\star$.  Hence $F_N$ is not SoS for every
$N\ge2m_\star$.  Taking
$
N_0:=2m_\star
$
proves the theorem.

\label{rem:explicit-threshold}
The main proof uses only
\Cref{lem:negative-limit,prop:R-vanishes}.
Given the complexity of obtaining an explicit
quantitative threshold, we additionally provide
exact computational checks and formal verification.
\Cref{prop:explicit-threshold} in Appendix~D provides an explicit

not SoS. This explicit large-order non-SoS result
has also been formally verified in Lean~4.
The bound is sufficient and is not claimed to be

the qualitative proof above.

label: lem:positive-split
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The Splitting Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices are orthogonal with respect to
the Frobenius inner product.  In particular,
\[
 \langle S,K_x\rangle_F=0,
 \qquad
 \|S_x+K_x\|_F^2
 =
 \|S_x\|_F^2+\|K_x\|_F^2.
\]
Moreover, $[S,S_x]$ is skew-symmetric, whereas $[S,K_x]$ is symmetric.
Hence
\[
 \|[S,S_x+K_x]\|_F^2
 =
 \|[S,S_x]\|_F^2+\|[S,K_x]\|_F^2.
\]
Substitution into the definition of $F$ proves the first identity.
For the second identity, use
$
\langle K,S_x\rangle_F=0
$
and the fact that $[K,S_x]$ is symmetric, while $[K,K_x]$ is
skew-symmetric.  The same argument then gives the second identity.
head: environment

label: lem:positive-mixed
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Symmetric--skew-symmetric pair

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\langle S,K\rangle_F=0$,
$
 F(S,K)=2\lVertS\rVert_F^2\lVertK\rVert_F^2-\lVertSK-KS\rVert_F^2.
$
For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^N$, the exterior-product Lagrange
identity gives
\[
 \frac12\lVertv\rVert^2\lVertK\rVert_F^2-\lVertKv\rVert^2
 =
 \sum_{i<j<k}
 (v_i k_{jk}-v_j k_{ik}+v_k k_{ij})^2.
\]
This identity follows directly by expansion.
Apply it to each column of $S$ and sum to obtain
\[
 2\lVertS\rVert_F^2\lVertK\rVert_F^2
 =
 4\lVertKS\rVert_F^2
 +
 4\sum_{\ell=1}^N\sum_{i<j<k}
 (s_{i\ell}k_{jk}-s_{j\ell}k_{ik}+s_{k\ell}k_{ij})^2.
\]
Finally, $(SK)^\top=-KS$, so
$\lVertSK\rVert_F=\lVertKS\rVert_F$.
The parallelogram identity therefore yields
$
 4\lVertKS\rVert_F^2-\lVertSK-KS\rVert_F^2
 =
 \lVertSK+KS\rVert_F^2.
$
Combining the two identities proves
\eqref{eq:positive-mixed}.
Every entry of $SK+KS$, and every expression inside the
remaining squares, is a homogeneous quadratic polynomial
in the independent entries of $S$ and $K$.
head: environment

label: prop:same-symmetry
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Both symmetric or skew-symmetric pair

title: Proof
body_md:
In either case, the matrices are determined by their nonnegative
diagonal parameters. We use the wedge coordinates introduced in
\Cref{subsec:wedge-coordinates}. Set $m=N-1$ and reverse the nonzero
diagonal labels by writing
\[
 \hat z_{ab}=z_{N-b,N-a},
 \qquad 1\le a<b\le m.
\]
This indexing replaces the diagonal-length weights
$(N-a)(N-b)$ by $ab$.
We rewrite the Toeplitz form as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-reduction}
 \begin{aligned}
 F^{\rm sym}(X,Y)
 =
 4N\sum_{b=1}^{N-1}(N-b)z_{0b}^2
 +4\Psi_{N-1}(\hat z),\qquad
 F^{\rm skew}(X,Y)
 =4\Psi_{N-1}(\hat z).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Note that the full calculation is given in
Appendix \ref{app:same-symmetry-reduction}.
Here $\Psi_m(\hat z)$ is defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-reduced-form}
 \Psi_m(\hat z)
 :=
 2\sum_{1\le a<b\le m}ab\,\hat z_{ab}^2
 -
 \sum_{\delta=1}^{m-1}
 \sum_{\substack{k\ge0\\2k<m-\delta}}
 \left(
   \sum_{p=k+1}^{m-\delta-k}\hat z_{p,p+\delta}
 \right)^2.
\end{equation}
Intuitively, the inner sum in
\eqref{eq:positive-reduced-form} selects a window from the sequence
$
\hat z_{1,1+\delta},\ldots,\hat z_{m-\delta,m},
$
successively removing $k$ terms from each end. 
All we need to prove next is that
$\Psi_m(\hat z(x,y))$ is SoS. For example, when $m=4$ and $\delta=1$,
the two windows give
\[
 (\hat z_{12}+\hat z_{23}+\hat z_{34})^2
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \hat z_{23}^2.
\]
The essential observation is that the wedges satisfy the Pl\"ucker
relations recalled in \Cref{subsec:wedge-coordinates}. These relations
allow the cross terms in the negative window squares to be re-paired
without changing the polynomial in $x,y$. For instance,
\[
 -2\hat z_{12}\hat z_{34}
 =
 -2\hat z_{13}\hat z_{24}
 +2\hat z_{14}\hat z_{23}.
\]
Applying the prescribed re-pairing rule gives three types of
squares: window sums along a fixed index total, differences of
wedges with the same gap, and individual wedges.
\Cref{prop:positive-window-certificate} gives the
complete identity and its coefficients. The window and
difference terms have nonnegative integer weights.
After allocating the diagonal terms to these squares, the
remaining coefficient of $\hat z_{p,p+\delta}^2$, denoted
$s_\delta(p)$ in Appendix \ref{app:positive-windows}, satisfies
$
 s_\delta(p)\ge p^2>0.
$
This estimate ensures that completing the squares leaves no
negative remainder. 
Consequently, $\Psi_m$ is a sum of squares of linear combinations
of the wedges, after using their Pl\"ucker relations.
Since each wedge is quadratic in $x,y$, this is an SoS
representation in the original variables.
Equation~\eqref{eq:positive-reduction} proves both assertions.

name: Proof sketch

label: thm:one-sided
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:one-sided}
For every $N\ge2$, the Toeplitz B\"ottcher--Wenzel form $F(X,Y)$ is SoS
whenever either $X$ or $Y$ is symmetric or skew-symmetric Toeplitz.
The other factor may be an arbitrary real Toeplitz matrix.
head: environment
name: One symmetric or skew-symmetric factor

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $X$ is symmetric Toeplitz.  By
\Cref{lem:positive-split},
$
 F(X,Y)=F(X,S_y)+F(X,K_y),
$
where the two terms are SoS by \Cref{prop:same-symmetry} and
\Cref{lem:positive-mixed}, respectively.  The skew-symmetric case is
identical with the two results interchanged.  Finally,
$F(X,Y)=F(Y,X)$ gives the same conclusion when the structural
assumption is imposed on $Y$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The splitting above relies on one factor having a fixed symmetry. If
both factors are decomposed into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts,
additional cross terms appear and the four resulting BW forms no longer
give the whole expression. 
Indeed, let $X=S_1+K_1$ and $Y=S_2+K_2$, with
$S_1,S_2$ symmetric and $K_1,K_2$ skew-symmetric.
Expanding the two Frobenius-orthogonal parts of
the commutator gives
\[
F(X,Y)=F(S_1,S_2)+F(K_1,K_2)+F(S_1,K_2)+F(K_1,S_2)+\mathcal C,
\]
where $
\mathcal C
= -4\langle S_1,S_2\rangle_F
       \langle K_1,K_2\rangle_F -2\langle[S_1,S_2],[K_1,K_2]\rangle_F -2\langle[S_1,K_2],[K_1,S_2]\rangle_F.
$
For Toeplitz matrices, the four displayed $F$ terms admit
SoS representations by the results above. The term
$\mathcal C$ vanishes if one factor has only one symmetry
part, but is present in general. Thus the argument proves
the one-sided result above, but does not extend directly
to unrestricted Toeplitz pairs. No sign or SoS assertion
for $\mathcal C$ is needed in the one-sided proof.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite-positive}
For every integer $2\le N\le50$, $F_N$ is a sum of squares of real

head: environment
name: The finite positive range

title: Proof
body_md:
At order two, direct expansion gives
$
 F_2=4z_{-1,0}^2+4z_{0,1}^2.
$
Suppose $F_n=\sum_j q_j^2$, where the $q_j$ are real homogeneous
quadratics. Since $\mathbf H_n\succeq0$, it admits a real factorization
$\mathbf H_n=V_n^\top V_n$. Equation~\eqref{eq:finite-chain} gives
\[
 F_{n+1}
 =
 \sum_j\bigl(\sqrt{\alpha_n}\,q_j\circ\psi_n\bigr)^2
 +
 \sum_i\bigl(V_nz^{(n+1)}\bigr)_i^2.
\]
Each factor is again a homogeneous quadratic. Induction through
$n=49$ therefore proves the result for every $2\le N\le50$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $r=\binom m2$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{1. Reduction of the Gram family.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}, every Gram representation of $\mathcal{F}_m$
differs from the fixed representation
\[
G_m=
\begin{pmatrix}
D&K&0\\
K&D&0\\
0&0&B
\end{pmatrix}
\]
by Pl\"ucker corrections.  We classify these corrections according to
how their four labels are distributed between the two sides of the
Toeplitz corner.

Four labels on the same side produce corrections acting entirely within
one pure wedge family.  Such a correction has entries
$
(\mathcal E_0)_{ab,cd}=\Omega_{abcd},
$
where $\Omega$ is totally antisymmetric in its four indices.  These are
the same-side Pl\"ucker corrections, or equivalently the pure
four-forms.

Two labels on each side produce the Pl\"ucker relations that couple the
two pure families with the mixed family.  After the pure cross
correction is collected into a symmetric matrix
$
\mathcal E_1\in\mathbb S^r,
$
the corresponding change in the mixed block is determined by the same
Pl\"ucker relations.  We denote this induced matrix by
$
\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1\in\mathbb S^{m^2}.
$
Equivalently, after antisymmetrically extending the entries of
$\mathcal E_1$ in each pure index pair, the realignment map is given by
\[
 (\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1)_{ac,bd}
 =(\mathcal E_1)_{ab,cd},
 \qquad
 (\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1)_{ad,bc}
 =-(\mathcal E_1)_{ab,cd}.
\]
Thus $\mathcal{R}$ simply re-pairs the four indices from the two pure wedge
pairs into two mixed wedge pairs.

Corrections involving three labels on one side and one label on the
other produce pure--mixed blocks.  To remove these terms, change the
sign of all variables on the negative side.  This transformation leaves
the pure coordinates $u,v$ unchanged and changes the sign of every
mixed coordinate $w$.  The polynomial $\mathcal{F}_m$ is unchanged, so if
$Q\succeq0$ is a Gram representation, averaging $Q$ with its image
under this symmetry preserves both the represented polynomial and
positive semidefiniteness, while eliminating all pure--mixed blocks.

Next interchange the two sides of the Toeplitz corner.  Under this
symmetry,
\[
                         (u,v)\longmapsto(-v,-u),
 \qquad
                         w_{ab}\longmapsto-w_{ba}.
\]
A second averaging therefore makes the two pure diagonal corrections
equal and makes the pure cross correction symmetric.  Consequently,
whenever a positive semidefinite Gram representation exists, there is
one of the form in \eqref{eq:general-gram-1}.  Both averaging operations
are convex averages of positive semidefinite matrices and therefore
preserve positive semidefiniteness.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{2. Block diagonalization.}
Write
$
 A:=D+\mathcal E_0, 
 C:=K+\mathcal E_1.
$
Then the two pure blocks of $Q_{\rm av}$ have the form
$
 \begin{pmatrix}
 A&C\\
 C&A
 \end{pmatrix}.
$
Consider the orthogonal matrix
$
 U=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \frac1{\sqrt2}I_r&\frac1{\sqrt2}I_r&0\\
 \frac1{\sqrt2}I_r&-\frac1{\sqrt2}I_r&0\\
 0&0&I_{m^2}
 \end{pmatrix}.
$
It corresponds to the change of coordinates
$
 (u,v,w)
 \longmapsto
 \left(
 \frac{u+v}{\sqrt2},
 \frac{u-v}{\sqrt2},
 w
 \right).
$
Since $U^\top U=I$, direct multiplication gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 U^\top Q_{\rm av}U
  =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 A+C&0&0\\
 0&A-C&0\\
 0&0&B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1
 \end{pmatrix}                                                 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 D+\mathcal E_0+K+\mathcal E_1&0&0\\
 0&D+\mathcal E_0-K-\mathcal E_1&0\\
 0&0&B+\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
{                                 This proves} \eqref{eq:general-gram-2}--\eqref{eq:sectors}.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{3. Equivalence with the SoS condition.}
Suppose first that $\mathcal{F}_m$ is SoS.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}, it has a
positive semidefinite Gram representation in the restricted wedge
coordinates.  Part~1 shows that this representation can be replaced,
without losing positive semidefiniteness, by one of the form
\eqref{eq:general-gram-1}.  Thus there exist
$\mathcal E_0,\mathcal E_1$ for which $Q_{\rm av}\succeq0$. 
Conversely, if such matrices $\mathcal E_0,\mathcal E_1$ exist and
$Q_{\rm av}\succeq0$, then
$
Q_{\rm av}=R^\top R
$
for some real matrix $R$.  Since $Q_{\rm av}$ is a Gram representation
of $\mathcal{F}_m$,
$
 \mathcal{F}_m
 =z_r^\top Q_{\rm av}z_r
 =\|Rz_r\|^2,
$
which is a sum of squares of homogeneous quadratic polynomials.
Therefore
\[
 \mathcal{F}_m\text{ is SoS}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists\,\mathcal E_0,\mathcal E_1
 \text{ such that }Q_{\rm av}\succeq0.
\]
Finally, $U$ is orthogonal, so
\[
 Q_{\rm av}\succeq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 U^\top Q_{\rm av}U\succeq0.
\]
By the block diagonal form in Part~2, this is equivalent to
$
                         P_+\succeq0, 
                         P_-\succeq0, 
                         M\succeq0.
$
This proves the lemma.

label: B:lem:scaled-limit
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Scaled Gram-invariant limit

label: B:eq:denominators
title: Proof
body_md:
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_m(\xi,\eta,\zeta,\omega)
= f(\xi,\eta)^\top Df(\zeta,\omega{                                 )} +v_3(\xi,\eta)^\top
  (B+\mathcal{R}(D-K))v_3(\zeta,\omega).
\end{aligned}
\]
The symbol $L_\infty$ denotes the absolutely convergent four-variable
series obtained by extending all depth indices in this fixed
Gram-invariant kernel to nonnegative integers; it does not denote
a finite matrix. For these four-slot generating kernels set
\begin{equation}\label{B:eq:denominators}
 A=(1-\xi\zeta)(1-\eta\omega),\quad
 C=(1-\xi\eta)(1-\zeta\omega),\quad
 \Delta=(1-\xi\omega)(1-\eta\zeta).
\end{equation}
Summing the fixed blocks $D,K,B$ and their realignments using
$\sum_{a\ge0}(a+1)t^a=(1-t)^{-2}$ and the common-shift
minimum-kernel identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{B:eq:generating}
 L_\infty(\xi,\eta,\zeta,\omega)
 =2\left(\frac2{A^2}+\frac1{C^2}
                 -\frac1{AC}-\frac2{\Delta^2}\right).
\end{equation}
The quantities $A,C,\Delta$ in this equation are four-variable
denominators, distinct from the indexed limits $A_{\ell h},C_{\ell h}$.
The finite-depth coefficients are bounded by a constant multiple
of a degree-four polynomial in the depth indices. Every term omitted by truncation has
at least one depth index at least $m$. Splitting the radial decay
in half and summing the resulting geometric tails yields
\begin{equation}\label{B:eq:qualitative-L-tail}
 |L_m-L_\infty|\le C_0 m^4 e^{-c_0\sqrt m}=o(m^2)
\end{equation}
for the fixed test nodes, with constants $C_0,c_0>0$
independent of $m$. The corresponding explicit constants
are derived separately in \Cref{D:lem:quant-tails}.
At the test pairs $\mathsf x_\ell^{(m)},\mathsf x_h^{(m)}$,
write
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_m^{\ell h} &=(1-\xi_\ell^{(m)}\bar\xi_h^{(m)})
                   (1-\eta_\ell^{(m)}\bar\eta_h^{(m)}),\\
 C_m^{\ell h} &=(1-\xi_\ell^{(m)}\eta_\ell^{(m)})
                   (1-\bar\xi_h^{(m)}\bar\eta_h^{(m)}),\\
 \Delta_m^{\ell h} &=(1-\xi_\ell^{(m)}\bar\eta_h^{(m)})
                   (1-\eta_\ell^{(m)}\bar\xi_h^{(m)}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $1-e^{-\epsilon z}=\epsilon z+O(\epsilon^2)$ uniformly
for the fixed test set, we have
\[
 mA_m^{\ell h}\to A_{\ell h},\qquad
 mC_m^{\ell h}\to C_{\ell h},\qquad
 \Delta_m^{\ell h}\to4,
\]
where $A_{\ell h},C_{\ell h}$ are given in
\Cref{lem:negative-limit}. Combining these limits with
\eqref{B:eq:generating} and \eqref{B:eq:qualitative-L-tail} yields
\[
 m^{-2}(\mathbf L_m)_{\ell h}
 \to2\left(\frac2{A_{\ell h}^2}
     +\frac1{C_{\ell h}^2}-\frac1{A_{\ell h}C_{\ell h}}\right).
\]
As the number of test points is fixed, entrywise convergence
implies convergence in every matrix norm.

label: B:lem:witness
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Exact negative direction

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the entries in \eqref{B:eq:entry} are rational, the quadratic
form can be checked using integer arithmetic only.  Define
\[
 \mathcal J
 :=
 \sum_{\ell,h\in I}
 \left\lfloor
 \frac{2^{64}d_\ell d_h
 \bigl(4C_{\ell h}^2+2A_{\ell h}^2
       -2A_{\ell h}C_{\ell h}\bigr)}
 {A_{\ell h}^2C_{\ell h}^2}
 \right\rfloor.
\]
Each summand is rounded toward $-\infty$.  Since $|I|^2=2^{20}$,
\[
 \frac{\mathcal J}{2^{64}}
 \le d^\top\mathbf L_\star d
 \le \frac{\mathcal J+2^{20}}{2^{64}}.
\]
Hence\footnote{
The exact integer evaluation is
$
 \mathcal J
  =-111807741093765987869670624504700,   
 \mathcal J+2^{20}
  =-111807741093765987869670623456124$ whose upper numerator is smaller than $-2^{106}$.
}
$d^\top\mathbf L_\star d<-2^{42}$.  The stated $\ell_1$ norm follows
directly from \eqref{B:eq:witness}. 
Now
$
 \|d\|_2^2\le\|d\|_1^2<2^{60}.
$
Therefore the Rayleigh quotient satisfies
$
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf L_\star)
 \le \frac{d^\top\mathbf L_\star d}{\|d\|_2^2}
 <-\frac{2^{42}}{2^{60}}
 =-2^{-18}.
$

body_md:
The bound $2^{-18}$ in \eqref{B:eq:eig-margin}
should not be confused with numerical accuracy.
A direct floating-point computation gives

\approx -1.18428\times10^{-2},

conservative bound $-2^{-18}$.

to establish strict negativity rigorously,
independently of floating-point computations.

label: C:lem:conjugate
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{C:lem:conjugate}
For $\xi=ie^{-(\alpha+i\beta)/\sqrt m}$, with $\alpha,\beta$
in fixed compact real intervals and $\alpha$ bounded away from zero,
every feasible normal-form Gram representation satisfies
\[
 f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*P_-f(\xi,\bar\xi)=O(m),
\]
uniformly over those intervals and all feasible representations.
head: environment
name: Uniform conjugate-slice bound

label: C:eq:generating
title: Proof
body_md:
For fixed $m$, put
\[
 Q_{0,m}(\xi,\eta,\zeta,\omega)
 :=f(\xi,\eta)^\top(D-K)f(\zeta,\omega).
\]
We use $Q_{0,\infty}$ for the absolutely convergent four-variable
generating series obtained by extending the depth indices in this
kernel to all nonnegative integers; $D_\infty$ has the analogous
meaning for $D$. Thus neither symbol denotes a finite Gram matrix.
Using the denominators $A,C,\Delta$ defined in
\eqref{B:eq:denominators}, geometric-series summation gives
\begin{equation}\label{C:eq:generating}
\begin{aligned}
 D_\infty =2(A^{-2}-\Delta^{-2}), \qquad
 Q_{0,\infty} =D_\infty-\frac{2(\Delta-A)}{A\Delta C}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the first formula follows from
$\sum_{a\ge0}(a+1)t^a=(1-t)^{-2}$. For the pure cross block,
setting $b=a+j$, $d=c+j$, $j\ge1$, gives
\[
 \sum_{a,c\ge0}\min(a+1,c+1)(\xi\eta)^a(\zeta\omega)^c
     =\frac1{C(1-\xi\eta\zeta\omega)},
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{j\ge1}(\eta^j-\xi^j)(\omega^j-\zeta^j)
     =\frac{(1-\xi\eta\zeta\omega)(\Delta-A)}{A\Delta}.
\]
On conjugate nodes, the pure four-form has zero quadratic
evaluation and realignment gives
\begin{equation}\label{C:eq:repeated}
 f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*P_-f(\xi,\bar\xi)
 =f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*(D-K)f(\xi,\bar\xi)
  +v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)^*(M-B)v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi).
\end{equation}
If $\xi=\sqrt\rho e^{i\vartheta}$, substituting
$A=C=(1-\rho)^2$ and $\Delta=(1-\rho)^2+4\rho\sin^2\vartheta$
into \eqref{C:eq:generating} yields
\begin{equation}\label{C:eq:repeated-baseline}
 Q_{0,\infty}(\xi,\bar\xi,\bar\xi,\xi)
 =\frac{8\rho\sin^2\vartheta}
 {(1-\rho)^2((1-\rho)^2+4\rho\sin^2\vartheta)^2}.
\end{equation}
We next bound the finite-depth tails. Since $M\succeq0$ and
$B\succeq0$ have the same diagonal, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
gives, with $W=(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)(d+1)$,
\[
 |(M-B)_{ab,cd}|\le4\sqrt W\le4W.
\]
The coefficients of the fixed baseline kernel are also bounded
by a constant multiple of $W$. Every omitted finite-depth term
contains an index at least $m$; the cancellation
\eqref{eq:grouped-low-vanishing} leaves only total degrees at least
$m$ in both arguments of the mixed correction. For the prescribed
scaled nodes, the polynomially weighted geometric tails therefore give
\[
 \left|f(\xi,\bar\xi)^*(D-K)f(\xi,\bar\xi)
     -Q_{0,\infty}(\xi,\bar\xi,\bar\xi,\xi)\right|
 +\left|v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)^*(M-B)v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)\right|
 \le C_1m^4e^{-c_1\sqrt m}=o(m),
\]
with $C_1,c_1>0$ independent of the Gram representation.
Explicit uniform tail constants are proved in
\Cref{D:lem:quant-tails}.
Writing $\rho=e^{-2\alpha/\sqrt m}$ and
$\vartheta=\pi/2-\beta/\sqrt m$, we have
$(1-\rho)^2=4\alpha^2/m+O(m^{-3/2})$ and
$\sin^2\vartheta\to1$. Hence the expression in
\eqref{C:eq:repeated-baseline} is
$m/(8\alpha^2)+o(m)$ uniformly on the specified intervals.
Combining these facts with \eqref{C:eq:repeated} proves the lemma.

label: C:lem:continuation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{C:lem:continuation}
For each feasible Gram representation, let
$P_-=\Gamma^\top\Gamma$ and put
\[
 h_m(\alpha,\beta)
 =\frac1m\Gamma f\left(ie^{-(\alpha+i\beta)/\sqrt m},
 -ie^{-(\alpha-i\beta)/\sqrt m}\right).
\]
For all sufficiently large $m$, uniformly over feasible Gram
representations,
\[
 \|h_m(\alpha,\beta)\|^2\longrightarrow0
\]
throughout the fixed region
\begin{equation}\label{C:eq:speed-region}
 1\le\Re\alpha\le2,\quad |\Im\alpha|\le256,\quad
 |\Re\beta|\le256,\quad |\Im\beta|\le\tfrac12.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Uniform analytic continuation

label: C:eq:global
title: Proof
body_md:
We first obtain a global bound. The Pl\"ucker four-form cancels
when one adds the four nonnegative evaluations of $P_+$ and $P_-$
at $(\xi,\eta)$ and $(\xi,\bar\eta)$; their sum is
$
 2f(\xi,\eta)^*Df(\xi,\eta)
 +2f(\xi,\bar\eta)^*Df(\xi,\bar\eta).
$
Since each summand on the left is nonnegative and the two fixed
$D$-evaluations have geometric-series bounds, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{C:eq:global}
 0\le f(\xi,\eta)^*P_\pm f(\xi,\eta)
 \le\frac{C_0}{(1-|\xi|^2)^2(1-|\eta|^2)^2},
 \qquad |\xi|,|\eta|<1.
\end{equation}
Here $C_0$ is an absolute constant, independent of $m$ and of
the Gram corrections; the explicit value needed for the
finite threshold is derived in \Cref{D:lem:quant-continuation}.
This bound requires $P_+,P_-\succeq0$ and is uniform in the
Gram corrections. On fixed complex rectangles satisfying
$\Re\alpha-|\Im\beta|\ge1/4$, the two node moduli are
\[
 |\xi|=e^{-(\Re\alpha-\Im\beta)/\sqrt m},\qquad
 |\eta|=e^{-(\Re\alpha+\Im\beta)/\sqrt m}.
\]
Thus \eqref{C:eq:global} implies $\|h_m\|^2\le C_2$
for all sufficiently large $m$, independent of the Gram
representation. On the real rectangle
$\alpha\in[1/2,1024+1/2]$, $\beta\in[-512,512]$,
the two nodes are conjugate. By \Cref{C:lem:conjugate},
$\|h_m\|^2\le C_3/m$ uniformly there.

We use the two-constant principle, applied to the subharmonic
function $\log\|h_m\|^2$. Fix real $\beta\in[-512,512]$.
On the upper and lower $\alpha$-rectangles
\[
 \tfrac12\le\Re\alpha\le1024+\tfrac12,
 \qquad 0\le\pm\Im\alpha\le512,
\]
the global estimate holds on all sides and the real side has
$O(m^{-1})$ decay. The harmonic measure of the real side has a
positive lower bound on the compact region
$1\le\Re\alpha\le2$, $|\Im\alpha|\le256$.
The two-constant principle therefore gives $\|h_m\|^2=o(1)$
uniformly there, while $\beta$ remains real.
For fixed complex $\alpha$ in this region, apply the same argument
to the upper and lower $\beta$-rectangles
\[
 -512\le\Re\beta\le512,\qquad
 0\le\pm\Im\beta\le\tfrac34.
\]
These lie in $\Re\alpha-|\Im\beta|\ge1/4$, and their real
sides have the improved bound from the first continuation.
A second positive harmonic-measure bound gives $\|h_m\|^2=o(1)$
uniformly in the region \eqref{C:eq:speed-region}.
All bounds are independent of the dimension of $\Gamma$.

label: D:lem:quant-tails
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Quantitative finite tails

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $W=(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)(d+1)$.
The coefficients of $L_\infty$ and $Q_{0,\infty}$ are
bounded by a constant multiple of $W$; the diagonal and minimum
terms give bounds $2W$ for $D$, $2W$ for $K$, and $4W$ for $B$.
Every discarded finite-depth term contains at least one depth
index at least $m$. Split its radial decay in half, choose this
index in four ways, and use
\[
 \sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)e^{-\epsilon j/4}
 =(1-e^{-\epsilon/4})^{-2},\qquad
 1-e^{-\epsilon/4}\ge\epsilon/8.
\]
The resulting estimate is
$
 64e^{-\epsilon m/4}(1-e^{-\epsilon/4})^{-8}
 \le2^{30}\epsilon^{-8}e^{-\epsilon m/4},
$
which proves \eqref{D:eq:L-tail} and the fixed part of
\eqref{D:eq:P-tail}.
Since $\operatorname{diag}(\mathcal{R}\mathcal E_1)=0$, $M$ and $B$
have the same diagonal. Their positive semidefiniteness and
Cauchy--Schwarz give
$
 |(M-B)_{ab,cd}|\le4\sqrt W\le4W.
$
By \eqref{eq:grouped-low-vanishing}, its repeated generating
expression has total degrees at least $m$ in both groups. The
same weighted geometric summation bounds it by
\[
 \left|v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)^*(M-B)v_3(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)\right|
 \le2^{26}\epsilon^{-8}e^{-\epsilon m/2}.
\]
Combining these estimates with \eqref{C:eq:repeated} gives
\eqref{D:eq:P-tail}.
head: environment

label: D:lem:quant-continuation
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Quantitative analytic continuation

title: Proof
body_md:
By the four-evaluation cancellation in the proof of
\Cref{C:lem:continuation}, each nonnegative pure evaluation is
bounded by the two fixed $D$ evaluations. Summing the corresponding
geometric series gives the explicit bound
\[
 0\le f(\xi,\eta)^*P_\pm f(\xi,\eta)
 \le\frac{8}{(1-|\xi|^2)^2(1-|\eta|^2)^2}.
\]
Together with $1-e^{-\epsilon/2}\ge\epsilon/4$, this gives
$
 \|h_m(\alpha,\beta)\|^2\le2^{20}
$
whenever $\Re\alpha-|\Im\beta|\ge1/4$.
On the real conjugate slice
$\alpha\in[1/2,1024+1/2]$, $\beta\in[-512,512]$,
\eqref{C:eq:repeated-baseline}, \Cref{D:lem:quant-tails},
and \eqref{D:eq:dyadic-tails} improve this to
\[
 \|h_m(\alpha,\beta)\|^2\le2^{20}\epsilon^2.
\]
The two-constant principle applies to the subharmonic function
$\log\|h_m\|^2$ and is independent of Gram-factor dimension.
On the upper $\alpha$-rectangle
$1/2\le\Re\alpha\le1024+1/2$, $0\le\Im\alpha\le512$,
use the harmonic barrier
\[
 H_1(\alpha)=\sin\frac{\pi(\Re\alpha-1/2)}{1024}
 \frac{\sinh(\pi(512-\Im\alpha)/1024)}{\sinh(\pi/2)}.
\]
It vanishes on the other three sides and is between zero and one
on the real side. On $1\le\Re\alpha\le2$, $0\le\Im\alpha\le256$,
$H_1>2^{-12}>2^{-13}$. Reflecting gives
\[
 \|h_m(\alpha,\beta)\|^2\le
 2^{20}\epsilon^{2\cdot2^{-13}}
\]
for $1\le\Re\alpha\le2$, $|\Im\alpha|\le256$,
and real $\beta\in[-512,512]$.
For fixed such $\alpha$, apply the same argument to the upper
and lower $\beta$-rectangles, using
\[
 H_2(\beta)=\cos\frac{\pi\Re\beta}{1024}
 \frac{\sinh(\pi(3/4-\Im\beta)/1024)}{\sinh(3\pi/4096)}.
\]
On $|\Re\beta|\le256$ and $0\le\Im\beta\le1/2$,
$H_2>2^{-5}$. Since
$2\cdot2^{-13}\cdot2^{-5}=2^{-17}$, the second comparison,
followed by reflection, proves \eqref{D:eq:quant-continuation}.

label: thm:finite-scale
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Uniform finite-scale non-SoS test

label: eq:evaluated-gram
title: Proof
body_md:
Use the fixed data of \eqref{B:eq:witness}, and put
$\mathsf x_\ell=(\xi_\ell,\eta_\ell)
=(ie^{-\epsilon a_\ell},-ie^{-\epsilon\bar a_\ell})$.
Then $\eta_\ell=\bar\xi_\ell$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:evaluated-gram}
 \mathcal G_m=
 \left[
 \left(M+\frac{P_++P_-}{2}\right)(\overline{\mathsf x_\ell},\mathsf x_h)
 \right]_{\ell,h\in I},
 \qquad \Phi_m=\epsilon^4d^*\mathcal G_md.
\end{equation}
Each summand is an evaluated positive semidefinite kernel on the same
list of points. Taking the direct sum of the pure and mixed feature
spaces proves $\mathcal G_m\succeq0$, hence $\Phi_m\ge0$.

Let $\mathbf L_m$ and $\mathbf R_m$ be the evaluation matrices of
$L_m$ and $\mathcal{R} P_-$ at these points. Realignment gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:realigned-diagonal}
 (\mathcal{R} P_-)(\overline{\mathsf x_\ell},\mathsf x_h)
 =P_-(\bar\xi_\ell,\xi_h,\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h)
 =P_-[\bar\xi_\ell,\xi_h]=P_-[\xi_\ell,\bar\xi_h].
\end{equation}
The last equality uses real symmetry of $P_-$. For $\ell=(r,j,\sigma)$ and $h=(r',j',\sigma')$, take
\[
 \alpha=\frac{r+r'}2+i\frac{\sigma j-\sigma'j'}2,
 \qquad
 \beta=\frac{\sigma j+\sigma'j'}2-i\frac{r-r'}2.
\]
Then $\alpha+i\beta=a_\ell$ and $\alpha-i\beta=\bar a_h$.
These parameters satisfy \eqref{D:eq:speed-region}, so
\Cref{D:lem:quant-continuation} applies to every entry of
\eqref{eq:realigned-diagonal}. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:realigned-error}
 |\epsilon^4d^*\mathbf R_md|
 \le\lVertd\rVert_1^2\,2^{20}\epsilon^{2^{-17}}
 <2^{80}\epsilon^{2^{-17}}.
\end{equation}
It remains to compare the finite baseline with $\mathbf L_\star$. At the test
points, each factor of $A$ and $C$ has the form $1-e^{-\epsilon\chi}$,
where $\Re\chi\ge2$ and $|\chi|<2^{10}$.
The integral identity
\[
 \frac{1-e^{-\epsilon\chi}}{\epsilon\chi}
 =\int_0^1e^{-\epsilon\chi u}\,du
\]
and $|e^{-\epsilon\chi u}-1|\le\epsilon|\chi|u$ give a relative
error at most $2^{10}\epsilon$ for each factor. Thus
$A/\epsilon^2=A_0(1+\delta_A)$ and
$C/\epsilon^2=C_0(1+\delta_C)$, where
$|\delta_A|,|\delta_C|\le2^{12}\epsilon\le1/16$.

For $|\delta|\le1/4$ we use
$|(1+\delta)^{-1}-1|\le2|\delta|$ and
$|(1+\delta)^{-2}-1|\le6|\delta|$.
At our points $A_0,C_0\ge4$. Each factor of $\Delta$ is
$1+e^{-\epsilon\chi}$, and $|\Im(\epsilon\chi)|\le512\epsilon<1$,
so the exponential has positive real part and $|\Delta|\ge1$.
Writing $\delta=\max(|\delta_A|,|\delta_C|)$, the product of the two
inverse factors has relative error at most $5\delta$. The three reciprocal
terms in \eqref{B:eq:generating} therefore contribute at most
$(3/2+3/4+5/8)\delta<3\delta\le3\cdot2^{12}\epsilon$; the remaining
$\Delta$ term contributes at most $4\epsilon^4$. In particular,
\[
 |\epsilon^4 L_\infty(\overline{\mathsf x_\ell},\mathsf x_h)-\mathbf L_\star(\ell,h)|
 \le2^{20}\epsilon.
\]
All four node moduli are at most $e^{-\epsilon}$, so
\eqref{D:eq:L-tail} and \eqref{D:eq:dyadic-tails} add at most
$\epsilon$ to this scaled error. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-tangent}
 |\epsilon^4 L_m(\overline{\mathsf x_\ell},\mathsf x_h)-\mathbf L_\star(\ell,h)|
 \le2^{30}\epsilon.
\end{equation}
Pairing \eqref{eq:finite-decomposition} with $d$, and using
\Cref{B:lem:witness}, \eqref{eq:realigned-error} and
\eqref{eq:finite-tangent}, gives
\begin{align*}
 0\le\Phi_m
  =\epsilon^4d^*\mathbf L_md-\epsilon^4d^*\mathbf R_md <-2^{42}+2^{90}\epsilon+2^{80}\epsilon^{2^{-17}} =-2^{42}+2^{90}m^{-1/2}+2^{80}m^{-1/262144}.
\end{align*}
Here both entrywise errors are multiplied by
$\lVertd\rVert_1^2<2^{60}$, and $\epsilon=m^{-1/2}$.
This proves \eqref{eq:finite-scale}.

name: Explicit sufficient order

title: Proof
body_md:
Convexity of $x\mapsto2^{-x}$ gives
$2^{-x}\le1-x/2$ for $0\le x\le1$. The upper bound in
\eqref{eq:finite-scale} is therefore at most
$
 -2^{42}+2^{90-k}+2^{42}2^{-2^{-17}}
 \le-2^{24}+2^{90-k}<0.
$
This contradicts $\Phi_m\ge0$, so $\mathcal{F}_m$ is not SoS. By
\Cref{lem:corner}, it is a linear restriction of $F_N$ for every
$N\ge2m=2^{9961475}$, and any SoS representation of such an
$F_N$ would restrict to one of $\mathcal{F}_m$.

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: An explicit window decomposition

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p\ge1$, $1\le\alpha<\beta$ and
$p+\alpha+\beta\le m$, the Pl\"ucker identity is
\[
 R_{p,\alpha,\beta}
 :=\hat z_{p,p+\alpha}\hat z_{p+\beta,p+\alpha+\beta}
  -\hat z_{p,p+\beta}\hat z_{p+\alpha,p+\alpha+\beta}
  +\hat z_{p,p+\alpha+\beta}\hat z_{p+\alpha,p+\beta}=0.
\]
Add $2\kappa_\alpha(p,p+\beta)R_{p,\alpha,\beta}$ to
$\Psi_m$ for every such triple. These additions preserve the
polynomial. Their effect on the Gram entries is as follows.
For two wedges of the same gap $\delta$ at positions $p<q$,
write $e=q-p$. If $e>\delta$, the correction cancels the entry
$-\kappa_\delta(p,q)$. If $e<\delta$, it changes that entry to
$-\kappa_\delta(p,q)-\kappa_e(p,p+\delta)=-\omega_\delta(p,q)$.
If $e=\delta$, no four distinct indices are present and the entry
remains $-\omega_\delta(p,q)$.

The third product in $R_{p,\alpha,\beta}$ couples wedges on the
same antidiagonal. For $a<b$ in $I_\sigma$, its coefficient in
the Gram is
\[
 \kappa_{b-a}(a,\sigma-b)
 =\min(a,\sigma-b,m+1-b,m+1+a-\sigma)
 =t_\sigma(a,b).
\]
Counting the sets $\mathcal W_k^\sigma$ containing both $a$ and
$b$ expresses these entries by the first sum in
\eqref{eq:positive-window-certificate}. The second sum gives
the negative same-gap entries, and \eqref{eq:positive-slack}
makes the diagonals agree. All remaining entries are zero.
This proves the identity.

It remains to check the signs. Each tent value in its range is
a positive integer, so $\omega_\delta(p,q)\ge1$.
The bounds $\kappa_\delta(p,p)\le p$ and
$t_{2p+\delta}(p,p)\le p$ are immediate.
For a right neighbour at distance $e<\delta$ the edge weight
is at most $2p$, and at distance $e=\delta$ it is at most $p$.
For a left neighbour these bounds are $2(p-e)$ and $p-\delta$,
respectively. Including missing boundary neighbours only increases
the upper bound, whence
\[
 \sum_q\omega_\delta(\min(p,q),\max(p,q))
 \le
 \begin{cases}
 (2\delta-1)p+p(p-1),&p\le\delta,\\
 (4\delta-2)p-\delta^2,&p>\delta.
 \end{cases}
\]
Inserting these estimates into \eqref{eq:positive-slack} gives
\[
 s_\delta(p)\ge
 \begin{cases}
 p^2,&p\le\delta,\\
 p^2+(p-\delta)^2,&p>\delta.
 \end{cases}
\]
The sums in the certificate are finite because the windows are
eventually empty. Every wedge is quadratic in the original variables,
so the displayed identity is a finite sum of homogeneous quadratic
squares. Integer weights may equivalently be realized by repeating
the corresponding squares.
